content:
The Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China (the Alliance) is set to be sentenced on 21 August for its alleged incitement to subversion case. Li Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung, who pleaded not guilty, have been in remand for nearly five years due to this case. In the case, the Alliance's slogan "End one-party dictatorship," chanted for over 30 years, was accused by the prosecution as equivalent to "ending Communist Party leadership" and overthrowing or destroying the fundamental system of the state, constituting incitement to subvert state power by "illegal means." However, the defence rebutted that "End one-party dictatorship" merely demands an end to the illegitimate "party dictatorship" and the building of a democratic China, which does not equate to ending Communist Party leadership. The defendants harboured no hostility towards the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and had no subversive intent, and the prosecution also failed to specify what actions the Alliance advocated people take to "End one-party dictatorship." What exactly are the prosecution's allegations? How did the defence rebut them? How did the court handle disputes over issues such as the Chinese Constitution and the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown? On the eve of the verdict, Collective Reporting Society (集誌社) has compiled nine key points and controversies from the 24-day trial. Related reports on the Alliance case

The Alliance, its chairman Li Cheuk-yan, vice-chairmen Albert Ho and Chow Hang-tung are charged with incitement to subvert state power. The verdict will be handed down on 21 August.

控方的檢控基礎是什麼？

The Alliance, Li Cheuk-yan, Albert Ho and Chow Hang-tung are charged with "incitement to subvert state power," alleging that they incited others in Hong Kong to commit acts "aimed at subverting state power" by "illegal means," namely to overthrow or destroy the fundamental system of the state established by the Chinese Constitution, or to overthrow the central authorities. Among these, the prosecution defined "illegal means" as "ending the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party, violating the Chinese Constitution (particularly Article 1 and the Preamble)," treating so-called "violations of the Chinese Constitution" as "illegal."

The core of the charge lies in "End one-party dictatorship," one of the Alliance's five major goals. The prosecution argued that the Alliance promoted and disseminated the "End one-party dictatorship" message "in the name of so-called democracy or the June 4th incident," coupled with negative content targeting the state. Although there was no explicit or detailed plan, the "natural and reasonable effect" of the message is to "end the CCP's leadership."

The core of the prosecution's charge lies in "End one-party dictatorship," one of the Alliance's five major goals, which it claims is equivalent to ending CCP leadership.

The prosecution's logic is that Article 1 of the Chinese Constitution, amended in 2018, explicitly states: "The socialist system is the fundamental system of the People's Republic of China. The leadership of the Communist Party of China is the defining feature of Chinese socialism. No organisation or individual may undermine the socialist system." This reflects that CCP leadership is the "fundamental system of the state established by the Constitution," and there is "no legal means" to end it. Therefore, the defendants' advocacy of "End one-party dictatorship" necessarily constitutes incitement to subvert state power by "illegal means" that violate the Chinese Constitution.

However, this prosecutorial basis was rejected by the court during mid-trial submissions. The judges held that the issues were of great significance and far-reaching implications, but the prosecution's submissions were "superficial," lacking sufficient analysis or authoritative works, and without calling any expert witnesses. The court would not consider this. The court would only consider the prosecution's second basis: even if there were legal means to end CCP leadership, the Alliance was in substance not advocating constitutional amendment but inciting people to overthrow the Communist Party's leading position by unlawful means.

法庭應如何詮釋中國憲法？

The elements of the charge involve the Chinese Constitution, and how the court should interpret and apply the relevant provisions became critical. No Chinese constitutional expert was called to testify in this case. Chow Hang-tung pointed out that the power to interpret the Constitution lies with the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, and Hong Kong courts have no authority to interpret it. Furthermore, Hong Kong lawyers and judges are trained in common law and lack relevant expertise. Without expert evidence and without consensus between prosecution and defence, the court should not even interpret constitutional provisions literally.

The prosecution agreed that Hong Kong courts have no authority to interpret the Constitution, but argued that the wording is very clear and can be understood and applied literally without the need for expert evidence. Li Cheuk-yan's side also believed the court could interpret literally, but if the prosecution made submissions beyond the literal meaning, expert evidence would be required; otherwise, such submissions should not be accepted.

The judges ultimately ruled that constitutional provisions that can be directly applied in Hong Kong and are relevant to the case, including the Preamble and Article 1 relied upon by the prosecution, can be understood by the court according to their literal meaning and context to determine their obvious meaning as the basis for adjudication, but reliance on meanings beyond the literal text is not permitted.

The elements of the charge involve the Chinese Constitution. The prosecution did not call any expert witnesses, and the judges ruled that the obvious meaning could be understood according to literal meaning and context.

如何處理六四等政治議題？是非曲直是否相關？

The Alliance's prosecution inevitably brought political issues such as June 4th into the courtroom. In the opening statement, the prosecution stated that this is not a political trial and does not involve adjudication of any issues concerning democracy, June 4th, criticism of the state, history, or the merits of political systems. Whether the national constitution is democratic, as the defendants claim, or contains the negative content they allege, is "fundamentally irrelevant to the case and the court need not address it."

However, the prosecution also alleged that the defendants exploited current affairs topics to incite, using negative content to arouse hatred towards the regime to enhance incitement, and disseminated "End one-party dictatorship" through June 4th vigils and the museum. The judge at one point joked that the prosecution was accusing the Alliance of "selling dog meat under the label of mutton" (a Chinese idiom meaning misrepresenting the true nature), but the prosecution denied this, saying "we never said their content is false," and it "could be true." The focus, they said, is on using these events to provoke hostility towards the CCP and achieve the overthrow of Communist Party leadership.

The prosecution alleged that the defendants exploited current affairs topics for incitement and used venues such as the "June 4th Memorial Museum" to disseminate their message.

The prosecution's claims were denied by the defence. Li Cheuk-yan said the Alliance's actions were all protests against specific incidents, such as Liu Xiaobo's imprisonment, Liu Xia's house arrest, the 709 mass crackdown, and Li Wangyang's alleged suicide, and were not smears disguised in the name of democracy. Chow Hang-tung emphasised that June 4th was a real event, not fabricated or a smear campaign. The focus of the June 4th vigil was mourning, and the memorial museum was for preserving and spreading the truth. Accusing it of being set up to promote the goals is putting the cart before the horse: "June 4th has never been a tool we used to incite 'End one-party dictatorship'... It is lives, it is blood, it is crimes the government must face. It is not a tool to be exploited."

When Chow Hang-tung called witnesses to testify and attempted to describe what happened on June 4th, the judge repeatedly interrupted and stopped her, emphasising that the court would not judge the rights and wrongs of June 4th. Chow rebutted that the prosecution accused the defendants of smearing and fabricating lies, so basic facts were needed to determine whether the allegations were true. If it were established that the Alliance spoke the truth and its demands were well-reasoned, that falls within the scope of freedom of speech. However, the judge reiterated that the court cannot determine truth, stressing that this case is not about adjudicating June 4th but about whether the National Security Law has been violated: "I will not let you use this opportunity for political propaganda."

Politics cannot be discussed, but the prosecution uses political reasoning to infer the defendants' intent. When Li Cheuk-yan's side made closing submissions, they pointed out that if the court does not address the relevant issues and cannot judge whether criticism is justified, it should not conclude that the defendants used these issues to smear or cause hatred towards the CCP.

Chow Hang-tung emphasised that June 4th was a real event, stating that it "is lives, it is blood," not a tool to be exploited.

「結束一黨專政」等於「結束共產黨領導」？等於「推翻、破壞國家根本制度」？

The core of the prosecution's charge is essentially a string of equations: "End one-party dictatorship" = "End CCP leadership" = "Overthrow or destroy the fundamental system of the state." The defendants admitted to upholding "End one-party dictatorship," but contested that this equals "ending CCP leadership."

Li Cheuk-yan explained that the Alliance hoped to end the dictatorship, not CCP leadership, and that dictatorship and democracy are opposites. "End one-party dictatorship" means hoping that people will enjoy fundamental rights and establish a civil society, creating a foundation for discussing democracy, and letting the people decide whether the Communist Party continues to lead. "Whether the Communist Party leads is not for us to say, but for the people to say." He also cited remarks by former national leaders to support his point, such as Mao Zedong's promise after the founding of the nation not to implement one-party dictatorship, and Zhao Ziyang's statement that the Communist Party cannot monopolise governance.

During his testimony, Li Cheuk-yan quoted remarks by former national leaders, such as Mao Zedong's promise after the founding of the nation not to implement one-party dictatorship, and Zhao Ziyang's statement that the Communist Party cannot monopolise governance.

Chow Hang-tung pointed out that "one-party dictatorship" refers to a power structure, while "CCP leadership" refers to the actual power of a certain group. The two concepts are different and cannot be compared. "End one-party dictatorship" means demanding the return of power to the people and ending the state where the party is above the law. It does not equate to "ending CCP leadership," but equates to "building a democratic China."

The prosecution once questioned whether the defendants' call for "End one-party dictatorship" amounted to demanding a change of ruling party or "dynastic change." However, both reiterated that the position was that the people should decide whether the Communist Party governs, and that party rotation under a democratic system is normal.

Even if "End one-party dictatorship" were equivalent to "ending CCP leadership," the defence also contested the equation with "overthrowing or destroying" the fundamental system of the state. The defence argued that "overthrow" implies bringing down, using force, or making drastic changes to the order by abnormal means, while "ending" does not imply bringing down; for 30 years, the Alliance has gradually promoted human rights, merely advocating the slogan without concrete action, which cannot be called "overthrowing." "Destroy" carries malicious intent, but the Alliance focuses on facts and exercises civil rights; even if this harms the CCP's leading position, it does not constitute "destruction."

The defence also questioned the claim that CCP leadership is the fundamental system of the state. Chow Hang-tung pointed out that the Constitution does not literally grant the CCP any actual power; the prosecution's claim that the CCP dominates everything merely reflects political reality. There is only one fundamental system of the state, namely the socialist system, which can encompass various elements. When interpreting the Constitution, the founding principles must be considered and cannot be derived literally alone. She argued that since the court has restricted itself to literal interpretation of the Constitution, it cannot determine whether the prosecution's interpretation is correct; and if the Constitution's fundamental principle is democratic constitutionalism, calling for an end to one-party dictatorship cannot be unconstitutional.

Chow Hang-tung and Li Cheuk-yan's side repeatedly pointed out that the prosecution had never specified what actions the Alliance advocated people take to "End one-party dictatorship."

被告有否煽動人用「非法手段」？控方如何確立被告用「非法手段」？

The prosecution's basis is that the Alliance was not advocating constitutional amendment, but inciting people to overthrow Communist Party leadership by "illegal means." "Illegal means" is an important element of the charge in the case, and the defence argued this is the "fatal flaw" of the case, as the prosecution has been unable to specify what actions the Alliance advocated people take to "End one-party dictatorship."

Li Cheuk-yan testified that he supported "End one-party dictatorship" but would not tell people to take action: "We would not say 'do something to end one-party dictatorship.'" What they urged people to do were specific actions, such as signing petitions demanding the release of Liu Xiaobo or sending Christmas cards to prisoners. Chow Hang-tung also pointed out that work such as June 4th vigils, the memorial museum, and human rights advocacy already had their inherent purposes and meanings—they were practices of the five major goals, not inciting others to do anything. Li Cheuk-yan's side argued in closing submissions that the Alliance played a supportive and educational role, and said that if the Alliance truly incited people to take concrete action, it would be "a real failure," because in 30 years, regardless of how many people participated in rallies and marches, nothing in Hong Kong had been implemented as pushed by the Alliance to achieve the end of one-party dictatorship.

Chow Hang-tung also emphasised that one-party dictatorship is a power structure, not the rule of a particular party, and can only be ended by democratic and rule-of-law means. Ordinary people can only use indirect methods, such as evidence collection and preservation, public education and empowerment, and public opinion pressure, to attempt to break the monopoly from the bottom up. She cited Albert Ho's article "How to End One-Party Dictatorship," which mentioned three paths: leaders' self-reform, violent revolution, and peaceful civil resistance. The Alliance rejected violent revolution and has engaged in peaceful resistance for many years, such as submitting reports to the UN Human Rights Council mentioning mainland China's human rights issues and offering various recommendations to the Chinese government—all calls to use rule of law and legal means to end one-party dictatorship: "Advocating that the thief must return what he stole, but never advocated beating up the thief to take it back."

Chow Hang-tung once called a housewife, Sham Lai-fong, to testify. She stated that she participated in the June 4th candlelight vigil and the late-May march as a citizen to mourn the dead.

The prosecution further questioned that the defendants had never mentioned constitutional amendment; however, Li Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung stated that they supported the democratic movement including constitutional amendment, and the Alliance's support for Charter 08 also reflected the aspiration for legitimate constitutional amendment.

Regarding the prosecution's claim that the "natural and reasonable effect" of the defendants' advocacy of "End one-party dictatorship" is to overthrow CCP leadership, Chow Hang-tung rebutted that the natural and reasonable effect of street station activities is to ask people to attend rallies; it does not become encouragement to commit "some unknown act that is unconstitutional and ends one-party dictatorship" merely because the slogan "End one-party dictatorship" is mentioned in the process. The citizen witness she called also testified that over the years they participated in rallies to mourn the dead, not because they认同 (agreed with) the five major goals and intended to do something specific; Li Cheuk-yan's side argued that Hong Kong citizens "are not fools" and it cannot be assumed that their understanding of "End one-party dictatorship" must be the same as the prosecution's.

Regarding the prosecution's definition of "illegal means" as "unconstitutional means," Li Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung emphasised that the Constitution constrains the government, not the people, and they did not believe ordinary people could violate the Constitution. The defence criticised the prosecution for "circular reasoning": defining violation of Article 1 of the Constitution as illegal means, and claiming that the subversive goal of "ending CCP leadership" violates Article 1, thus using "unconstitutionality" to prove both the goal and the means simultaneously—equivalent to saying the defendants "violated Article 22 of the National Security Law by means that violate Article 22 of the National Security Law."

被告有否煽動顛覆意圖？

The prosecution must prove "dual intent" in this case: that the defendants intended not only to incite others to commit subversive acts, but also to incite subversion itself. The prosecution inferred that the defendants possessed subversive intent based on their hostility towards the Communist Party; the defence denied this, emphasising that the goal was to build a democratic China, not subversion.

During cross-examination, Li Cheuk-yan agreed that he regarded the CCP as an authoritarian regime that suppressed the people and stifled democracy, but disagreed that he harboured extreme hostility towards the CCP, saying "I have no hostility in my heart, only love." He stated that his criticism was based on love for the people, hoping the Communist Party could reform so that the people could obtain their due rights. He described himself as "absolutely patriotic," hoping for a democratic, prosperous, and free nation where the people have a good future. The defence stressed that there was no evidence that Li Cheuk-yan was "saying one thing but meaning another."

Chow Hang-tung reiterated that advocating "End one-party dictatorship" means subverting the illegitimate party dictatorship, demanding accountability from those in power and "returning power to the people." She said the current accusation "is like us, as the masters of the country, telling a thief to return the stolen goods, only to be accused by the thief of robbery." The judge once asked whether she was placing the CCP in an adversarial position; she said she would not use the word "enemy": "As Mr Liu Xiaobo said, we have no enemies; what we resist is the system."

Chow Hang-tung said she would not use the word "enemy" to describe the CCP, quoting Liu Xiaobo: "We have no enemies; what we resist is the system."

是否明知「結束一黨專政」違法？

The prosecution alleged that after the National Security Law came into effect, the defendants knew "End one-party dictatorship" was illegal yet persisted. The defence denied this outright. Li Cheuk-yan said that at the time, he "believed I was absolutely not breaking the law," noting that for over 30 years no one had ever said "End one-party dictatorship" was problematic. After the National Security Law, no one or the police ever said the slogan violated the law, nor was the Alliance banned from operating on national security grounds. The 2021 June 4th vigil was banned on pandemic grounds, not national security grounds.

Chow Hang-tung admitted the Alliance had discussed how to respond to the National Security Law, but believed "fighting for democracy cannot be illegal" and the risk "could not be avoided." The final consensus was to uphold the five major goals. The judge pointed out that they were aware of legal risks at the time; Chow disagreed, saying she believed there was no legal violation but political risk, and feared the law might be used as a tool for political suppression.

Chow Hang-tung admitted that after the National Security Law was implemented, the Alliance discussed how to respond, and the final consensus was to uphold the five major goals.

「結束一黨專政」是否受言論自由保障？

The prosecution argued that freedom of speech is not absolute, and that the defendants' advocacy of "End one-party dictatorship," intended to incite the audience to subvert state power, had crossed the line of human rights protection.

Li Cheuk-yan's side pointed out that Article 41 of the Chinese Constitution protects citizens' right to criticise any state organs, including the Communist Party. The Alliance never called on people to use any means, including illegal means, to end the dictatorship, but merely chanted slogans and made political demands, which should be protected by freedom of speech. Chow Hang-tung also pointed out that in a society that respects freedom of speech, advocating political reform and criticising government actions is perfectly normal and necessary. The speech in question aims to limit and monitor power and is unwelcome to the government; the court must be vigilant against the government using speech as an excuse for overcharging.

During the trial, the court discussed whether the defendants' support for Liu Xiaobo and the Charter 08 he initiated, and their assistance to people in engaging in behaviour that might incur criminal liability in the mainland, constituted "illegal means" under the subversion charge.

煽惑人違反內地法律是否違國安法？

During their testimony, Li Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung mentioned supporting Charter 08 initiated by Liu Xiaobo and others. The judge was concerned that relevant persons had been convicted and imprisoned in the mainland, and asked whether the defendants were assisting people in engaging in behaviour that might incur criminal liability there. The judge noted that "illegal means" in the subversion charge refers to illegal acts in Hong Kong or the mainland, and suggested leaving this for submissions.

However, Li Cheuk-yan's side questioned that the prosecution's basis was violation of the Constitution, and never mentioned "violation of mainland criminal law" as illegal means. Illegal means should only involve Hong Kong law, and whether the defendants incited people to use means violating mainland criminal law to promote constitutional amendment should not be an issue in this case. The prosecution also clarified that "illegal means" only refers to violation of the Chinese Constitution, not criminal law, and that the incitement must occur in Hong Kong. The defendants must issue the inciting message in Hong Kong, with the audience being Hong Kong people receiving it in Hong Kong. It only needs to be proven that the audience received the inciting message; even if no act was carried out as a result, the charge can be proven.
